lines.say: Beyond a green star, close to a white sun, lived a people called the Steelypips. They had no quarrels and no lessons. They lived on, in, and under one machine.
It was a fine machine of gears and springs. They had built it from their own saved atoms.
We made it ourselves, so there is nothing in it to fix.
One day a comet came by, in a lace bonnet, with four long tails and a smell of almonds. She said she would burn them to the ground, as a start.
One moment, madam. This machine has no faults. Please leave, or you will be sorry.
She filled the sky with fire, until their old moon curled up at both tips. So the Steelypips wrapped their strongest fields around it, and threw the switch.
The sky cleared with a bang. All that was left of the comet was a bit of ash. The Steelypips went back to being pleased.
Some time later, something came down from the sky. Nobody knew what it was. It landed on the highest peak, very heavily, and nobody wanted a second look.
Pardon us, but this is a very good machine. Please move along.
It did not move. It did not attack either. It just stayed.
So, to save money, they sent a small scarechrome to frighten it.
Fear me. I am terrible. Fear me.
It hissed and spat and frightened itself a little. The thing stayed. It tried a second frequency, but its heart was not in it.
Something heavier, then. Hydraulic, with plenty of muscle, and a scarechrome on top for luck.
The great engine rolled out. It wound itself up, and counted down from four.
Oil bubbled and gears rattled. Not a scratch.
The Steelypips held a council of war. They built a machine to build a machine to build a machine so large that the nearest stars stepped back, with a servospook at its heart.
I am the servospook. I mean business.
It gathered all its strength, and let go.
When the dark cleared, there was only scrap metal, ticking as it cooled.
Each weapon had been bigger than the last. The thing was the same size.
Then we must be patient. We will send a cyberivy, to creep up quietly and take its time.
The ivy crept up as if it had nothing on its mind. It sent out a root, then another, and closed in from behind. It went exactly as planned, and when it was over, it was not over.
They made nets and glues, lassos and screws, traps and walls, and turned the machine upside down. Nothing helped.
This has never happened to us before. We do not know what to do with our hands.
Then someone came along on a vehicle nobody could name. It had a horse’s head, one bicycle wheel and a rocket’s tail. The rider was Trurl, out on one of his trips.
We tried everything. It is still there.
Did you try anything that was not a weapon?
What else is there? We have gears, springs, and force.
I can stay a little while, as an adviser. Is that agreeable?
Of course! Shall we bring hammers, artillery, dynamite? Coffee or tea? The vending machine makes both.
Coffee. Not for me, for the job. The rest, no.
Force has failed, so we will use forms.
I need paper and ink, stamps and seals, a teller’s window, a zinc spoon, a saucer, coffee, and a mailman. And something to write with.
We will fetch it!
Trurl sat down, and dictated the first notice.
Regarding the obstruction of these premises, under Form Four, subsection Q: all services to the occupant are withdrawn, pending review. Appeals must be in writing, on the correct forms.
He sealed it, stamped it, entered it in the ledger, and checked the register. Then he sent for the mailman.
The mailman took it away. They waited.
Was it delivered?
It was.
And the receipt?
Signed, on this line. And here is its appeal.
Once it took delivery of the first notice, it belonged to the paperwork.
Without reading the appeal, he sent it back. Across the front he wrote, in a hurry, wrong forms, and signed with a scrawl no one could read.
Now, to work.

The mailman ran all day. Trurl stamped and filed. The typewriter chattered, and an office grew out of nothing: stamps and rubber bands, paper clips, pigeonholes, filing cabinets, signs, coffee rings, cobwebs.
Notices went out, then reminders, then final demands.
It is smaller. It really is smaller.
Next, please. The window is closed. Come back in an hour.
The coffee went cold. An official was offered a bribe, and filed it. New cabinets arrived, and cobwebs reached from wall to wall.
The typewriter typed an order that the occupant must leave, and may not appeal.
Then Trurl stood up and threw it all out into deep space: the desks, the chairs, the stamps, the seals, the pigeonholes. Only the vending machine stayed.
What are you doing? We had grown used to it!
Take a look instead, friends.
They looked, and the thing was gone. It had shrunk and shrunk, until they needed a magnifying glass. All they could find was one small damp spot, where something had dripped.
But why throw out the papers, and pour out the coffee?
Throw it all out, or the office will start on you.
He nodded to them kindly, climbed onto his odd vehicle, and flew away, smiling.
